newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM Hasina says economy picking up.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM Hasina says economy picking up.

text.p: Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said on Saturday that Bangladesh's economy was picking up as her government had taken "positive steps" for development of the private sector.
Hasina listed the launching of private cellular telephones, allowing export processing zones in the private sector and adopting a new policy to woo foreign investors in petroleum sector.
"We are aware that despite the liberal and pragmatic policies of the government we still have miles to go," she told a seminar on foreign direct investment.
Hasina said she had streamlined the administration to speed up implementation of policies and programmes.

She said there had been a positive sign in the economy with the fiscal deficit remaining under 6.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), inflation stabilising at around 4.0 percent and industrial growth hovering at 9.0 percent.
"Private remittance reached $1.5 billion this year and is expected to increase... (and) foreign exchange reserve is now equal to three months imports," she said.

The Prime Minister said there was no restriction on the amount of investment on equity shares. A foreign investor can own 100 percent of equity shares without having any prior approval from the government, she said.
According to World Investment Report, the flow of foreign direct investment (FDI) into the country was $14 million in 1993 and $11 million in 1994.
FDI proposals increased to more than $1.5 billion in 1995/96 (July-June), according to official figures.
Industry Minister Tofael Ahmed said on Saturday Bangladesh's share in world trade was only 0.3 percent and he blamed developed countries for offering little excess to their markets.
The discrepancy exists because the devloped countries are not adhering to the Uruguay round agreement, he said.
"We are determined to root out bureacratic red tapes for speedy development," he said.
Yussuf Abdullah Harun, President of Federation of Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said Bangladesh expected $1.5 billion in direct foreign investment over a period of two to three years.
"Even this is far too low in comparison with facilities and incentives Bangladesh is offering to investors," he told the seminar.
"This is mainly because of (bureaucratic) red tape," he said.
